source: In some cases, parasites disseminate through the skin and present as multiple non-ulcerative nodules (diffuse cutaneous leishmaniasis, DCL) or propagate through the lymphatic system resulting in nasobronchial and buccal mucosal tissue destruction (mucosal leishmaniasis, ML) (Reithinger et al., 2007; Dedet and Pratlong, 2009).

evidence: This is supported by citations to Chamaille et al., 2010 and Ready, 2013.

claim: Infection in dogs is closely associated with human population density.
source: Furthermore, whilst significant anthroponotic transmission of L. donovani occurs across parts of the Old World, zoonotic cycles of VL, primarily tied to canine hosts, dominate L. infantum transmission (Chamaille et al., 2010; Ready, 2013), with infection in dogs shown to be closely associated with human population density.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the context of explaining VL distribution patterns.

claim: Important predictors of CL distribution differed markedly between the Old and New World.
source: Important predictors of CL distribution differed markedly between the Old and New World.
evidence: This is a result from comparing the BRT modeling results between regions.

claim: Peri-urban land cover was the most important predictor of CL in the Old World.
source: Whilst peri-urban land cover was the most important predictor of the disease in the Old World, in the New World temperature was the highest predictor, with abiotic factors predicting 74.18% of CL distribution.
evidence: This is a result from the BRT modeling analysis shown in Table 2.

claim: In the New World, temperature was the highest predictor of CL, with abiotic factors predicting 74.18% of CL distribution.
source: Whilst peri-urban land cover was the most important predictor of the disease in the Old World, in the New World temperature was the highest predictor, with abiotic factors predicting 74.18% of CL distribution.
evidence: This is a result from the BRT modeling analysis.

claim: The difference in the relative importance of climatic drivers between Old and New World CL reflects that in the Old World the main endemic CL areas are due to both anthroponotically transmitted L. tropica and zoonotic cycles of L. major, whereas in the New World the disease is primarily associated with sylvatic and zoonotic cycles with various Leishmania spp. and wild reservoir hosts.
source: This difference in the relative importance of climatic drivers reflects the fact that in the Old World the main endemic CL areas are due to both anthroponotically transmitted L. tropica and zoonotic cycles of L. major, whereas in the New World the disease is primarily associated with sylvatic and zoonotic cycles with a variety of different Leishmania spp. and wild reservoir hosts implicated (Ashford, 1996; Reithinger et al., 2007; WHO, 2010; Lima et al., 2013; Ready, 2013).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the modeling results supported by citations to Ashford, 1996; Reithinger et al., 2007; WHO, 2010; Lima et al., 2013; and Ready, 2013.

claim: The distribution maps represent a spatially refined assessment of the global environmental risk of leishmaniasis.
source: The distribution maps represent a spatially refined assessment of the global environmental risk of leishmaniasis and provide a starting point for various public health activities including targeting areas for control and assessing disease burden.
evidence: This is an evaluative claim about the study's contribution.

claim: The maps provide a starting point for various public health activities including targeting areas for control and assessing disease burden.
source: The distribution maps represent a spatially refined assessment of the global environmental risk of leishmaniasis and provide a starting point for various public health activities including targeting areas for control and assessing disease burden.
evidence: This is a claim about the potential applications of the study's outputs.

claim: The maps compare favourably to the WHO Expert Committee on the Control of Leishmaniases outputs.
source: The maps compare favourably to the WHO Expert Committee on the Control of Leishmaniases outputs (WHO, 2010), have high model validation statistics and improve upon the existing body of work by providing a finer resolution of risk at a subnational level.
evidence: This is a comparative evaluation with reference to WHO, 2010.

claim: The maps have high model validation statistics.
source: The maps compare favourably to the WHO Expert Committee on the Control of Leishmaniases outputs (WHO, 2010), have high model validation statistics and improve upon the existing body of work by providing a finer resolution of risk at a subnational level.
evidence: This refers to the AUC and correlation statistics reported in the Results section.

claim: The maps improve upon the existing body of work by providing a finer resolution of risk at a subnational level.
source: The maps compare favourably to the WHO Expert Committee on the Control of Leishmaniases outputs (WHO, 2010), have high model validation statistics and improve upon the existing body of work by providing a finer resolution of risk at a subnational level.
evidence: This is a claim about the advancement over previous work.

claim: The countries indicated by Alvar et al. (2012) as having 90% of all VL and 75% of all CL cases were all predicted by the maps to have risk for VL and CL, respectively.
source: Similarly, the countries indicated by Alvar et al. (2012) as having 90% of all VL and 75% of all CL cases, were all predicted by our maps to have risk for VL and CL, respectively.
evidence: This is a validation result comparing the study's predictions with known high-burden countries from Alvar et al., 2012.

claim: Northwest China is predicted to have high risk for VL, though low population densities and remoteness likely lead to few reported cases.
source: Regions such as Northwest China are predicted to have high risk for VL, though the low population densities in this area are likely to lead to very few cases and, given its remoteness, even fewer reported cases.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the modeling results in the context of population and reporting factors.

claim: The Mediterranean coastline of Europe is predicted to be highly suitable for leishmaniasis, but few human cases are observed.
source: Other regions, such as the Mediterranean coastline of Europe, are predicted to be highly suitable for leishmaniasis, but we see few human cases.
evidence: This is an observation about discrepancies between predicted risk and observed cases.

claim: The maps predict the probability of disease presence in an area, rather than directly infer measures of incidence or burden.
source: This is because the maps presented predict the probability of disease presence in an area, rather than directly infer measures of incidence or burden, which can be influenced by a variety of other factors (e.g., in the Mediterranean coastline of Europe, VL has been associated with immunosuppression).
evidence: This is an important clarification about what the maps represent.

claim: The evidence consensus layer acts as a rough filter on the environmental risk maps.
source: The evidence consensus layer, used to mask out regions with high consensus on leishmaniasis absence, acts as a rough filter on the environmental risk maps.
evidence: This describes how the evidence consensus layer is used in the analysis.

claim: In order to model the true relationship between environmental risk and disease incidence, a global data set of geopositioned disease incidence data would be required, which is currently unavailable.
source: However, in order to model the true relationship between environmental risk and disease incidence, a global data set of geopositioned disease incidence data would be required; at present this is unavailable.
evidence: This is an acknowledged limitation regarding data availability.

claim: Estimates of the populations living in areas of environmental risk are supplied as a proxy for the true burden of disease.
source: Estimates of the populations living in areas of environmental risk are therefore supplied as a proxy for the true burden of disease.
evidence: This clarifies what the population at risk estimates represent.

claim: Population at risk estimates cannot be directly compared with other global estimates of the leishmaniases' disease burden, such as the WHO estimates of clinical burden of around 350 million.
source: However, they cannot be directly compared with other global estimates of the leishmaniases' disease burden, such as the WHO estimates of clinical burden of around 350 million (WHO, 2010).
evidence: This is a clarification about the limitations of comparing different types of estimates, with reference to WHO, 2010.

claim: There is a strong, positive relationship between population at risk estimates and estimated annual incidence from Alvar et al. (2012).
source: Figure 4—figure supplement 4 shows a strong, positive relationship between population at risk estimates and estimated annual incidence from Alvar et al. (2012).
evidence: This is a result from the validation analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: Countries with indeterminate evidence consensus scores (e.g., Egypt, Nigeria, and Côte d'Ivoire) are exceptions to the positive relationship between population at risk and incidence, indicating a genuine lack of knowledge regarding both distribution and incidence.
source: The exceptions to this relationship (e.g., Egypt, Nigeria, and Côte d'Ivoire) are all countries with indeterminate evidence consensus scores, indicating a genuine lack of knowledge regarding both the distribution and incidence of disease.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the validation results in the context of the evidence consensus scores.

claim: Previous estimates of the leishmaniases' global burden have been complicated by poor knowledge of the global distribution of the diseases.
source: Previous estimates of the leishmaniases' global burden have been complicated by poor knowledge of the global distribution of the diseases (Bern et al., 2008; Reithinger, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bern et al., 2008 and Reithinger, 2008.

claim: The maps presented will help to increase the accuracy of future burden estimates.
source: It is hoped that the maps presented here will help to increase the accuracy of future estimates.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the future impact of the study.

claim: Species-specific models at the same level of detail as those presented are not currently possible due to a lack of suitable data.
source: Species-specific models at the same level of detail as those presented here are not currently possible due to a lack of suitable data.
evidence: This is an acknowledged limitation regarding the level of detail possible with current data.

claim: Developments in the use of 'big data' approaches to disease mapping may enable the construction of data sets which could be used for species-specific analyses.
source: Developments in the use of 'big data' approaches to disease mapping (such as the incorporation of informal internet resources) may enable the construction of data sets which could be used in these analyses (Hay et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a speculative claim about future possibilities, with reference to Hay et al., 2013.

claim: A further complication with burden estimation is the epidemic nature of the disease, leading to significant interannual variation in burden.
source: A further complication with burden estimation is the epidemic nature of the disease, as evidenced by the national case time series in Alvar et al. (2012), leading to significant interannual variation in burden.
evidence: This is supported by reference to evidence in Alvar et al., 2012.

claim: Any burden estimation would have to account for the epidemic nature and temporal spread of data would be critical.
source: Therefore, any burden estimation would have to account for this and the temporal spread of data would therefore be critical.
evidence: This is a recommendation for future burden estimation efforts based on the epidemic nature of the disease.

claim: Non-environmental drivers of transmission and morbidity, such as HIV immunosuppression and risk of infection via blood transfusions and intravenous drug usage, are not incorporated into the present models.
source: It should be noted that non-environmental drivers of transmission and morbidity, such as HIV immunosuppression and risk of infection via blood transfusions and intravenous drug usage, are not incorporated into our present models.
evidence: This is an acknowledged limitation of the modeling approach.

claim: The maps can help inform the wider discussion of non-environmental factors and their impact on leishmaniasis.
source: The maps presented here can help inform the wider discussion of these factors and their impact on leishmaniasis (e.g., by identifying regions with greater risk for HIV and leishmaniasis co-infection) (Desjeux and Alvar, 2003).
evidence: This is a claim about potential applications of the maps, with reference to Desjeux and Alvar, 2003.

claim: The niche based models could enable a decoupling of environmental from social factors to assess the importance of the latter on leishmaniasis transmission in particular areas.
source: Similarly, the niche based models used here could enable a decoupling of environmental from social factors to assess the importance of the latter on leishmaniasis transmission in particular areas.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential applications of the modeling approach.

claim: In some specific localities it may be non-environmental risk factors that are the main determinants of disease distribution.
source: It may indeed be the case that in some specific localities it is these non-environmental risk factors that are the main determinants of disease distribution.
evidence: This is a speculative statement acknowledging the potential importance of non-environmental factors in some locations.

claim: These maps represent evidence-based estimates of the current global distribution of the leishmaniases incorporating a comprehensive occurrence database and a rigorous statistical modelling framework with associated uncertainty statistics.
source: These maps represent evidence-based estimates of the current global distribution of the leishmaniases incorporating a comprehensive occurrence database and a rigorous statistical modelling framework with associated uncertainty statistics.
evidence: This is a summary claim about the study's contribution.

claim: 1.71 billion individuals live in areas that are suitable for CL transmission.
source: We estimate that 1.71 billion and 1.69 billion individuals live in areas that are suitable for CL and VL transmission, respectively.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the population at risk analysis.

claim: 1.69 billion individuals live in areas that are suitable for VL transmission.
source: We estimate that 1.71 billion and 1.69 billion individuals live in areas that are suitable for CL and VL transmission, respectively.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the population at risk analysis.

claim: The population at risk figures highlight the need for much greater awareness of leishmaniasis at a global scale.
source: These figures highlight the need for much greater awareness of this disease at a global scale.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the significance of the population at risk estimates.

claim: These maps provide an important baseline assessment and a strong foundation on which to base future burden estimates, target regions for control efforts and inform public health decisions.
source: These maps provide an important baseline assessment and a strong foundation on which to base future burden estimates, target regions for control efforts and inform public health decisions.
evidence: This is a summary claim about the potential applications and impact of the study.

claim: A boosted regression tree (BRT) modelling framework was used to generate global predicted environmental risk maps for CL and VL.
source: A boosted regression tree (BRT) modelling framework was used to generate global predicted environmental risk maps for CL and VL.
evidence: This describes the methodological approach used in the study.

claim: The methodology for generating the definitive extents for the leishmaniases was adapted from work on dengue.
source: The methodology used for generating the definitive extents for the leishmaniases was adapted from work on dengue (Brady et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Brady et al., 2012.

claim: Four primary evidence categories were used to determine a consensus on the presence or absence of the leishmaniases: health reporting organisations, peer-reviewed evidence of local autochthonous transmission, case data, and supplementary information.
source: Four primary evidence categories were used to determine a consensus on the presence or absence of the leishmaniases: (i) health reporting organisations; (ii) peer-reviewed evidence of local autochthonous transmission; (iii) case data; (iv) supplementary information.
evidence: This describes the methodological approach for the evidence consensus.

claim: Information was collected at provincial level (Admin 1 units) to better capture the focal nature of the leishmaniases.
source: Information was collected at provincial level (termed Admin 1 units by the Food and Agriculture Organization's (FAO) Global Administrative Unit Layers (GAUL) coding (FAO, 2008)) to better capture the focal nature of these diseases.
evidence: This describes the spatial resolution chosen for the analysis with reference to FAO, 2008.

claim: A threshold value of 12 CL cases and 7 VL cases in a given province in a given year was deemed suitable to distinguish significant disease events from sporadic cases.
source: A threshold value of 12 CL cases and 7 VL cases in a given province in a given year was deemed suitable by the authors to distinguish significant disease events from sporadic cases within that region.
evidence: This describes a methodological decision made by the authors.

claim: Healthcare expenditure per capita was used as a proxy to determine genuine sporadic reporting from inadequate surveillance.
source: This was used as a proxy to determine genuine sporadic reporting from inadequate surveillance.
evidence: This describes the rationale for using healthcare expenditure in the evidence consensus scoring.

claim: The Brazilian Ministry of Health produces records of infections at the municipality level via the SINAN reporting network.
source: The Brazilian Ministry of Health produces, via the Sistema de Informação de Agravos de Notificação (SINAN, 2013) reporting network, records of infections at the municipality level.
evidence: This describes a data source with reference to SINAN, 2013.

claim: The Brazilian data allowed for a more thorough evidence consensus to be performed at district level (Admin 2) within Brazil.
source: This allowed for a more thorough evidence consensus to be performed at district level (termed Admin 2 FAO, 2008) within Brazil.
evidence: This describes how the Brazilian data enabled finer spatial resolution analysis.

claim: From literature searches, 4845 articles were collated with data recorded at the resolution of either a point or Admin 1 or 2 polygon.
source: From these searches, 4845 articles were collated, with data recorded at the resolution of either a point or Admin 1 or 2 polygon.
evidence: This describes the scope of the literature review.

claim: As of December 2012, a total of 690 leishmaniasis relevant articles were archived in HealthMap.
source: As of December 2012, a total of 690 leishmaniasis relevant articles were archived.
evidence: This describes the number of records obtained from HealthMap.

claim: In total, 563 GenBank accessions were associated with sub-national location details and added to the database.
source: In total, 563 accessions were associated with sub-national location details and added to the database.
evidence: This describes the number of records obtained from GenBank.

claim: Information about 3465 strains isolated from humans was provided from the CNR-L archives, collected from between 1954 and 2013.
source: In total, information about 3465 strains isolated from humans was provided, collected from between 1954 and 2013.
evidence: This describes the number and temporal range of records from CNR-L.

claim: Occurrences were standardised annually to remove intra-annual duplicates, so that each individual record represented an occurrence of leishmaniasis infections in a given 5 km × 5 km location or administrative unit for one given year.
source: All data were geopositioned as precisely as possible, which resulted in both point-level data (referring to cities, towns or villages) as well as polygon-level data (provinces or districts) with area no greater than one square decimal degree. All data that had been manually geopositioned were checked to ensure coordinates were plausible and then occurrences were standardised annually to remove intra-annual duplicates, so that each individual record used in our model represented an occurrence of leishmaniasis infections in a given 5 km × 5 km location or administrative unit for one given year.
evidence: This describes the data processing methodology.

claim: The occurrence data were independent of burden; a location with 200 cases in one year has equal weighting in the model as a location with just one reported case.
source: As a result, the occurrence data were independent of burden; a location with 200 cases in one year has equal weighting in the model as a location with just one reported case, since it was only the presence of the disease being modelled.
evidence: This describes an important characteristic of the modeling approach.

claim: Humidity and moisture have often been identified as important for the sandfly, with humidity influencing breeding and resting.
source: Humidity and moisture, whether from rainfall or in the soil, have often been identified as important for the sandfly, with humidity influencing breeding and resting (Ready, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ready, 2013.

claim: Of the few sandfly breeding sites that have been identified, high humidity seems to be a common trait, including moist Amazonian soils, caves, animal burrows, and select human dwellings.
source: Whilst relatively little is known about these breeding sites, of the few that have been identified, high humidity seems to be a common trait, including moist Amazonian soils, caves, animal burrows, and select human dwellings (Killick-Kendrick, 1999; Feliciangeli, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Killick-Kendrick, 1999 and Feliciangeli, 2004.

claim: Studies have indicated soil type and their moisture profiles as determinants of sandfly distribution.
source: Studies have indicated soil type and their moisture profiles as determinants of sandfly distribution (Bhunia et al., 2010; Elnaiem, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bhunia et al., 2010 and Elnaiem, 2011.

claim: Precipitation represents a good global proxy measure for moisture.
source: Precipitation represents a good global proxy measure for moisture, and has been shown to play a prominent role in shaping disease distribution in previous leishmaniasis modelling efforts (Thomson et al., 1999; Elnaiem et al., 2003; Bhunia et al., 2010; Chamaille et al., 2010; Gonzalez et al., 2010, 2011; Elnaiem, 2011; Hartemink et al., 2011; Malaviya et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous modeling studies.

claim: Temperature influences both the development of the infecting Leishmania parasite in the sandfly as well as the life cycle of the sandfly vectors.
source: Temperature influences both the development of the infecting Leishmania parasite in the sandfly (Hlavacova et al., 2013) as well as the life cycle of the sandfly vectors.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hlavacova et al., 2013.

claim: Studies have shown that with increasing temperatures, the metabolism of the sandfly increases, influencing oviposition, defecation, hatching, and adult emergence rates.
source: On one hand, studies have shown that with increasing temperatures, the metabolism of the sandfly increases, influencing oviposition, defecation, hatching, and adult emergence rates (Kasap and Alten, 2005; Benkova and Volf, 2007; Guzman and Tesh, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kasap and Alten, 2005; Benkova and Volf, 2007; and Guzman and Tesh, 2000.

claim: Higher temperatures have been shown to increase mortality rates of adult sandflies.
source: On the other hand, higher temperatures have also been shown to increase mortality rates of adults (Benkova and Volf, 2007; Guzman and Tesh, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Benkova and Volf, 2007 and Guzman and Tesh, 2000.

claim: Studies have integrated the effects of temperature on sandfly biting rates, sandfly mortality, and extrinsic incubation periods to produce maps of how the basic reproductive number of canine leishmaniasis varied spatially.
source: Studies have integrated the effects of temperature on sandfly biting rates, sandfly mortality, and extrinsic incubation periods to produce maps of how the basic reproductive number of canine leishmaniasis varied spatially (Hartemink et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hartemink et al., 2011.

claim: Multiple studies have implicated temperature (including maximum, minimum, and mean temperatures) as being an important explanatory variable for both sandfly and disease distribution.
source: Multiple studies have also implicated temperature (including maximum, minimum, and mean temperatures) as being an important explanatory variable for both sandfly and disease distribution (Thomson et al., 1999; Gebre-Michael et al., 2004; Bhunia et al., 2010; Chamaille et al., 2010; Fischer et al., 2010; Galvez et al., 2011; Fernandez et al., 2012; Branco et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Vegetation provides many roles in sandfly habitat and survival, ranging from maintaining the necessary moisture profile for both immature stages and adults, to a sugar resource for both male and female sandflies.
source: Vegetation provides many roles in sandfly habitat and survival, ranging from maintaining the necessary moisture profile for both immature stages and adults, to a sugar resource for both male and female sandflies (Killick-Kendrick, 1999; Feliciangeli, 2004; Ready, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Killick-Kendrick, 1999; Feliciangeli, 2004; and Ready, 2013.

claim: Vegetation is an important resource for many mammals that sandflies feed on, and that potentially are Leishmania reservoirs.
source: Moreover, vegetation is an important resource for many mammals that sandflies feed on, and that potentially are Leishmania reservoirs.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the ecological relationships.

claim: NDVI has been implicated as a key explanatory variable in the distribution of leishmaniasis cases in several studies.
source: NDVI has been implicated as a key explanatory variable in the distribution of leishmaniasis cases in several studies (Cross et al., 1996; Thomson et al., 1999; Elnaiem et al., 2003; Gebre-Michael et al., 2004; Elnaiem, 2011; Hartemink et al., 2011; Bhunia et al., 2012; Toumi et al., 2012; de Oliveira et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Neglected tropical diseases and poverty are often found to be linked.
source: Neglected tropical diseases and poverty are often found to be linked and the use of a purely economic variable was chosen to act as a proxy for a variety of important global risk factors for disease, including malnutrition, housing quality, and living with domesticated animals (Bern et al., 2010; Boelaert et al., 2009; Herrero et al., 2009; Malafaia, 2009; Zeilhofer et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: An economic variable was chosen to act as a proxy for a variety of important global risk factors for disease, including malnutrition, housing quality, and living with domesticated animals.
source: Neglected tropical diseases and poverty are often found to be linked and the use of a purely economic variable was chosen to act as a proxy for a variety of important global risk factors for disease, including malnutrition, housing quality, and living with domesticated animals (Bern et al., 2010; Boelaert et al., 2009; Herrero et al., 2009; Malafaia, 2009; Zeilhofer et al., 2008).
evidence: This describes the rationale for including economic data, supported by multiple citations.

claim: Over the last few decades, there has been a tendency for the leishmaniases having a sylvatic/zoonotic transmission cycle to transition into the urban and peri-urban environment in response to increasing urbanisation trends.
source: Over the last few decades, there has been a tendency for the leishmaniases having a sylvatic/zoonotic transmission cycle to transition into the urban and peri-urban environment in response to increasing urbanisation trends (Harhay et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Harhay et al., 2011.

claim: The increasing overlap in habitat between suitable human and animal hosts and multiple available resting sites for adults can allow for transmission of disease to occur relatively easily.
source: The increasing overlap in habitat between suitable human and animal hosts and multiple available resting sites for adults can allow for transmission of disease to occur relatively easily (Singh et al., 2008; Poche et al., 2011; Uranw et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Singh et al., 2008; Poche et al., 2011; and Uranw et al., 2013.

claim: Boosted regression tree modelling combines regression trees and boosting to best capture the variables that define the distribution of the input data.
source: Boosted regression tree modelling combines both regression trees, which build a set of decision rules on the predictor variables by portioning the data into successively smaller groups with binary splits (De'ath, 2007; Elith et al., 2008), and boosting, which selects the tree that minimises the loss of function, to best capture the variables that define the distribution of the input data.
evidence: This describes the BRT methodology with citations to De'ath, 2007 and Elith et al., 2008.

claim: The core BRT setup followed standard protocol already defined elsewhere.
source: The core BRT setup followed standard protocol already defined elsewhere (Elith et al., 2008; Bhatt et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Elith et al., 2008 and Bhatt et al., 2013.

claim: There is no general consensus on how best to generate pseudo-data for species distribution modeling.
source: There is no general consensus on how best to generate pseudo-data (Bhatt et al., 2013); however, several factors of the generation process are known to influence the predicted distribution and thus can be sources of potential bias (Phillips et al., 2009; Van Der Wal et al., 2009; Phillips and Elith, 2011; Barbet-Massin et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bhatt et al., 2013; Phillips et al., 2009; Van Der Wal et al., 2009; Phillips and Elith, 2011; and Barbet-Massin et al., 2012.

claim: Pseudo-absence selection was directly related to the evidence consensus layer and restricted to a maximum distance from any occurrence point.
source: In order to minimise such effects, pseudo-absence selection was directly related to the evidence consensus layer and restricted to a maximum distance (μ) from any occurrence point.
evidence: This describes the methodological approach for generating pseudo-absences.

claim: Pseudo-presence data was incorporated, informed by the evidence consensus layer, to compensate for poor surveillance capacity in low prevalence regions.
source: Pseudo-presence data was also incorporated, again informed by the evidence consensus layer, to compensate for poor surveillance capacity in low prevalence regions.
evidence: This describes the methodological approach for generating pseudo-presences.

claim: Points were randomly located in regions above an evidence consensus threshold of −25, with regional placement probability weighted by evidence consensus scores.
source: As in Bhatt et al. (2013) points were randomly located in regions above an evidence consensus threshold of −25, with regional placement probability weighted by evidence consensus scores, so that regions with higher evidence consensus contained more pseudo-presences than lower scoring areas.
evidence: This describes the specific methodology for pseudo-presence generation with reference to Bhatt et al., 2013.

claim: By referencing the evidence consensus layer for pseudo-data selection, detection bias was mitigated.
source: By referencing the evidence consensus layer for pseudo-data selection, detection bias was also mitigated.
evidence: This is a claim about how the methodology addresses a potential source of bias.

claim: There is no definitive procedure for choosing the best number of pseudo-data points to generate the most accurate predictive map.
source: There is no definitive procedure for choosing the best number of pseudo-data points to generate the most accurate predictive map.
evidence: This is stated as an acknowledged limitation in the field.

claim: An ensemble BRT model was constructed with multiple BRT submodels fitted using pseudo-data points generated using different combinations of parameters.
source: To account for the impact that these parameters might have on the model predictions, an ensemble BRT model was constructed with multiple BRT submodels fitted using pseudo-data points generated using different combinations of parameters na, np, and μ.
evidence: This describes the ensemble modeling approach used to address uncertainty in pseudo-data generation.

claim: All combinations of parameter values resulted in a total of 75 individual input data sets and BRT submodels making up the BRT ensemble.
source: All combinations of these parameter values resulted in a total of 75 (5na × 3np × 5μ) individual input data sets and BRT submodels (making up the BRT ensemble).
evidence: This is a quantitative description of the ensemble modeling approach.

claim: For each disease, the 75 BRT submodels were used to predict a range of different risk maps, which were combined to produce a single mean ensemble risk map.
source: For each disease, the 75 BRT submodels were used to predict a range of different risk maps (each at 5 km × 5 km resolution), and these were combined to produce a single mean ensemble risk map for each disease, also allowing for computation of the associated range of uncertainty in these predictions for every 5 km × 5 km pixel as shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Figure 4—figure supplement 1.
evidence: This describes how the ensemble predictions were generated, with reference to uncertainty figures.

claim: For both diseases, the New World and Old World were modelled separately to account for and explore any differences in the epidemiology of the diseases between these regions.
source: For both diseases, the New World (the Americas) and Old World (Eurasia and Africa) were modelled separately in order to account for and explore any differences in the epidemiology of the diseases between these regions.
evidence: This describes the rationale for separate regional models.

claim: Separate modeling of Old and New World was done to differentiate the potential effect that different vectors (Lutzomyia spp. in the New World and Phlebotomus spp. in the Old World) and their varying life histories might have on disease distribution.
source: This was done to differentiate the potential effect that the different vectors namely Lutzomyia spp. in the New World and Phlebotomus spp. in the Old World and their varying life histories, might have on the distribution of the diseases within these regions.
evidence: This describes the rationale for separate regional models based on vector differences.

claim: Relative importance in BRT is defined as the number of times a variable is selected for splitting, weighted by the squared improvement to the model as a result of each split and averaged over all trees.
source: Relative importance is defined as the number of times a variable is selected for splitting, weighted by the squared improvement to the model as a result of each split and averaged over all trees (Friedman, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Friedman, 2001.

claim: The area under the receiver operator curve (AUC) reflects the ability to discriminate between presence and absence.
source: To evaluate the ensemble's predictive performance, we used the area under the receiver operator curve (AUC) (Fleiss et al., 2003)—the area under a plot of the true positive rate versus false positive rate, reflecting the ability to discriminate between the presence and absence.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Fleiss et al., 2003.

claim: An AUC value of 0.5 indicates no discriminative ability, and a value of 1 indicates perfect discrimination.
source: An AUC value of 0.5 indicates no discriminative ability, and a value of 1 indicates perfect discrimination.
evidence: This is an explanation of how to interpret AUC values.

claim: The distribution modelling technique assesses pixel level risk, rather than population level risk.
source: It is important to note that this distribution modelling technique assesses pixel level risk, rather than population level risk.
evidence: This is an important clarification about what the modeling approach measures.

claim: The ensemble evaluates the likelihood of leishmaniasis presence based upon the covariates supplied.
source: As such, the ensemble evaluates the likelihood of leishmaniasis presence based upon the covariates supplied.
evidence: This describes what the model outputs represent.

claim: Some factors such as national healthcare provisioning and standards of living will influence the true observed burden.
